name: Recurring leaderboard / bake-off content formats that drove community engagement
what_it_is: Content formats where model comparison is packaged as a recurring, shareable artifact rather than a one-time utility. Four real precedents with distinct mechanics: (1) Chatbot Arena / LMArena -- crowdsourced anonymous pairwise 'battles' where users prompt two hidden models, vote for the better answer, and models are ranked by an Elo-style score; the vote stream is continuous so the leaderboard is always live and self-updating. (2) Aider's polyglot leaderboard -- a fixed, reproducible benchmark of 225 Exercism coding exercises across 6 languages that the maintainer re-runs on each new model; its authority comes from testing real code-editing on identical tasks with cost data, updated on an ongoing basis (last updated Nov 2025). (3) dubesor's personal LLM benchmark table -- one person's manual 83-task suite scored A-grade-style across Pass/Refine/Fail/Refusal and topic categories, run once per model shortly after release, presented as an interactive sortable/filterable/exportable HTML table; ran 02/2024-04/2026 across 347 model entries before retiring. (4) r/LocalLLaMA recurring 'best model' / megathreads -- community-sourced, cadence-driven discussion threads where members post what actually runs well on their hardware. The shareable hook in each: a single comparable score/grade, a fixed format people learn to read, and a cadence (continuous, per-release, or weekly/monthly).
real_precedent: Chatbot Arena / LMArena (lmarena.ai, now arena.ai); Aider polyglot leaderboard (aider.chat/docs/leaderboards); dubesor.de LLM benchmark table; r/LocalLLaMA recurring benchmark/megathreads. All real and independently browsable.
evidence_of_impact: LMArena became deeply embedded in AI development -- major labs (OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta) supply models and route preview releases through it (DeepSeek prototypes, GPT-5 codename, Google's 'Nano Banana'); it incorporated in 2025, raised a $100M seed ($600M valuation) then a $150M Series A ($1.7B post-money), and rebranded to Arena in Jan 2026 -- strong evidence the recurring vote-battle format drove durable engagement (exact cumulative vote/model counts not fetched [uncertain]). Aider's leaderboard is a widely cited coding-model reference, actively maintained (entries 2024-2025, last update Nov 20 2025) and reproducible on 225 real exercises. dubesor's table ran consistently for ~2 years across 347 model entries / 203 with cost data before the creator retired it, explicitly citing 'thousands of hours' of manual effort and stating 'whatever comes next must be automated, within a rigorous framework.' r/LocalLLaMA had roughly 686,000 members at time of research, making its recurring threads a high-reach informal benchmark [uncertain member count].
applicability_to_agentdyno: AgentDyno's `dyno doctor` already emits an A-F grade plus agentic tool-calling pass/fail -- that grade is the exact 'single comparable score' hook that makes Aider's and dubesor's formats shareable. A realistic recurring format: 'This week's grade-A local models on a Goose/Cline tool-calling exam' or an 'F-vs-B bracket', generated by scripting `dyno pull` + `dyno serve` + `dyno doctor --json` across a FIXED small roster of models on a SINGLE published hardware profile, then rendering the results into a sortable/filterable/exportable table -- mirroring dubesor's presentation but with AgentDyno's tool-calling-verification niche as the differentiator (nobody else grades local models specifically on agentic tool-calling reliability against Goose/Cline). To stay sustainable, borrow the two survival lessons directly: (a) Aider's fixed-task reproducibility (same exam, same hardware profile, so results are comparable release-to-release), and (b) dubesor's explicit warning that manual testing across hundreds of models is unsustainable -- so AgentDyno's edge is that the exam is ALREADY automated via `dyno doctor`, letting one operator regenerate the whole table by re-running the pipeline rather than hand-scoring. Optionally add a light community-submission path (like Aider's 'contributing results') where users run `dyno doctor` on their own hardware and submit JSON, turning single-hardware limitation into a multi-hardware crowdsourced grid -- a nod to LMArena's crowdsourcing without needing a hosted vote server.
build_effort: medium. The exam engine (`dyno doctor`) and backend orchestration (`pull`/`serve`/`switch`) already exist, so the recurring-content layer is: (1) a batch runner that iterates a pinned model roster and collects `dyno doctor --json` per model (small), (2) a table/leaderboard renderer -- static HTML like dubesor's sortable table, or a markdown table for a recurring post (small-medium), and (3) if crowdsourced, a schema + intake for user-submitted doctor JSON plus a hardware-profile field, which is where effort grows toward large (validation, dedup, anti-gaming). Producing the content itself is cheap once the batch runner exists; the ongoing cost is operator time to actually run new models each cadence.
risk_or_caveat: 1) Hardware cost is the core constraint the task flags: every exam needs real local hardware and time, so a weekly cadence across many models is exactly the treadmill that burned out dubesor ('thousands of hours', then retirement) -- AgentDyno must keep the roster small and the hardware profile fixed, or automate ruthlessly, or the format dies. 2) Comparability/gaming: a single-operator single-hardware table invites 'your numbers don't match mine' disputes; crowdsourced submissions raise anti-gaming and hardware-normalization problems (LMArena itself has documented manipulation/methodology criticism). 3) Novelty decay: dubesor noted diminishing usefulness as models converged and eval gaps closed -- a grade table can become boring once top models all score A, so the tool-calling/agentic angle (where models still fail visibly) must stay the focus to keep it interesting. 4) Crowded space: LMArena and Aider are entrenched general references, so AgentDyno should not try to be a general leaderboard -- its only defensible recurring hook is 'local models graded on agentic tool-calling reliability, on named consumer hardware,' which none of the incumbents cover.
